title: Cropping is the worst way to make a photo square for a neural network
paper_title: Reshaping inputs for convolutional neural network: Some common and uncommon methods
date_note: Pattern Recognition 93: accepted 9 April 2019, available online 10 April 2019 (from the published PDF header)
authors: Swarnendu Ghosh, N Das, M Nasipuri
summary: Most image networks want square pictures of one fixed size. We trained 450 networks to compare 25 ways of squaring up a photo, and found that cropping, the usual choice, did worst.

body.p: Most image-recognition networks only accept pictures of one fixed size, usually a square. Real photos come in all shapes, so something has to give before a picture goes in. We tested 25 ways of turning a rectangular image into a square, on six datasets and three well-known networks, to see which ones help and which ones hurt.

A convolutional neural network (CNN) is the standard kind of network for pictures. It slides small filters over an image to pick out patterns. The layers near the end expect a fixed number of values, and that number depends on the size of the input. So a network built for 224 × 224 pixels cannot simply take a 4:3 photo. Inception-V3 expects 299 × 299 instead.

This causes trouble in practice. Images gathered by crowd-sourcing or web crawling come in many sizes. Phone cameras differ in resolution and in portrait or landscape mode. And a network pre-trained on ImageNet and reused for, say, surveillance footage has to be fed the shape it was trained on. The usual answer is to reshape the picture first. How much each way of reshaping matters to a CNN had not been explored much.

body.h2: Twenty-five ways to make a square

body.p: We grouped the methods into four families, shown in the figure below on one photo of a bird.

ul: Interpolation stretches the whole image into a square, using nearest-neighbour, bilinear, bicubic or Lanczos resampling. All the content is kept, but the proportions of objects are distorted and edges lose some quality. A white ball can start to look like an egg.
Cropping cuts a square out of the image, from the top or left, the centre, or a random position. Shapes stay true, but the rest of the picture is thrown away.
Redundant methods repeat the picture along its short side, either as tiles or as mirror images, until the square is full. These are rare in CNN work.
Noisy methods shrink the picture to fit inside a square and fill the leftover space with black, white, random pixels, or pixels copied at random from the image itself (clone fill).

figure.alt: A tall photo of a bird of prey and the results of the reshaping methods on it. Interpolation squashes it into a square, cropping keeps only a square window, tiling and mirroring repeat the bird side by side, and the fill methods place it in a square padded with black, white, random or cloned pixels.
figure.caption: One tall photo, reshaped by each family of methods, at the top-left, centre and random positions where that applies. The top right zooms in on how the four interpolation types differ.

body.p: Positions matter for every method except interpolation. We tried the top or left edge, the centre, and a random position that changes with every training epoch. Counting those variants gives the 25 methods.

We used six datasets: Bangla compound characters, Devanagari characters, street-view house numbers (SVHN), Indian movie faces (IMFDB), and objects cropped out of PASCAL and LabelMe photos. Each was split 3:1:1 into training, validation and test sets, with the same number of images per class. The networks were ResNet-18, Inception-V3 and DenseNet-121, with 11.7 million, 27.2 million and 8.0 million parameters (Table 3). Six datasets, three networks and 25 methods make 450 networks, each trained from scratch for 100 epochs, with a single run per setting.

Raw accuracy varies a lot between datasets, so we scaled the test accuracy of each dataset to run from 0 (worst method) to 1 (best method). We did the same for how many epochs a network needed to reach its lowest validation loss. We did not aim for record accuracy, only a fair comparison.

body.callout: Cropping converged fastest but scored lowest on test accuracy, so we advise against it unless you already know where the region of interest is.

body.p: Randomised positioning gave better test accuracy than fixed positions, in all three networks, though it took longer to converge. Seeing a different framing each epoch acts like data augmentation, which means making new training examples out of old ones. The effect was clearest for the natural-object datasets IMFDB, LabelMe and PASCAL.

Mirroring beat tiling on test accuracy. In ResNet-18 and Inception-V3 it also converged more slowly, which we put down to the same augmenting effect. We advise against mirroring for characters and text, because a flipped letter may change meaning, although the results showed this only weakly. Interpolation did better than cropping but fell short of the other families, especially on PASCAL, where stretching distorts the objects. Noisy methods did quite decently, but no fill method won consistently across the networks.

figure.alt: Three line charts, one per network (ResNet-18, Inception v3, DenseNet-121), showing relative test accuracy from 0 to 1 for each of the 25 reshaping methods. Each of the six datasets has a thin coloured line and the average is a thick black line. The average dips sharply at the three cropping positions.
figure.caption: Relative test accuracy of each reshaping method for each network. The thick black line is the average over datasets, and it drops sharply at the cropping positions.

body.p: The network matters too. Inception-V3 and DenseNet-121 proved more tolerant of interpolation than the shallower ResNet-18. Nearest-neighbour interpolation was the weakest interpolation choice for ResNet and DenseNet, but not for Inception-V3. Chi-square tests at the 0.05 level showed that several choices, such as the interpolation technique and the position of the crop or fill, depend on the dataset (Table 4). The paper adds that the natural-object datasets reacted more to the choice of interpolation method than the character datasets did.

Every result is a single training run, because 450 networks were already a lot of training and averaging over repeated runs would have taken too long. The study covers six datasets and three networks, all trained from scratch without pre-training. The main plots show relative scores, scaled within each dataset, and the actual accuracies are given in a supplementary figure (Fig. 11). The paper offers guidance for choosing a reshaping method, not one winner for every case.

The paper aims to give empirical evidence for choosing a reshaping method, and the official code is on GitHub. We also suggest that the same kind of study could be extended to ask how the inner workings of a network relate to the data it sees.
